prompt: Carrie started to draw a cat. A picture of her unfinished drawing is shown on the right. She finishes her drawing by adding more elements. Which of the figures below can show the finished drawing?
The Mayan people wrote numbers with dots and bars. A dot is written for 1 and a bar for 5. How did they write 17?
In how many ways can the word KENGA be read in the figure on the right if neighbouring letters of the word must lie in triangles that have a common side?

solutions.title: Start from every K
solutions.body:
There are three K's in the figure. Try each one and follow neighbours (triangles sharing a side) through E → N → G → A.

- **K in the top row:** its E neighbour is the E to its left. That E touches an N (top-left corner), that N touches the G below it, and that G touches **two** A's (left and right of it). → **2 ways**.
- **K on the far left (third row):** it has no E next to it. → 0 ways.
- **K in the middle of the third row:** it touches three E's.
  - The E on its left leads down to the N in the bottom row, then to the G beside it, then to the A in the bottom-right corner. → **1 way**.
  - The E above it leads to the N on its right, then up to the G in the top-right corner, then to the A beside that G. → **1 way**.
  - The E on its right leads to an N with no G next to it. → 0 ways.

Total: $2 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 4$.

**Answer: (B) 4**

solutions.title: Work backwards from the A's
solutions.body:
- Every path must end with G → A, and before that N → G. So first find the G's that touch both an N and an A.
- Then check whether that N touches an E, and that E touches a K.
- Doing this carefully, the G in the second row (touching the top-left N) gives 2 paths (it touches two A's), the G in the top-right corner gives 1 path, and the G in the bottom row (next to the bottom-right A) gives 1 path. The other G's dead-end.
- So there are $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$ readings of KENGA.

**Answer: (B) 4**

prompt: There are 14 girls and 12 boys in a kindergarten. One day, half of the children went out for a walk. At least how many of them are girls?

You see a numerical puzzle on the right. You have to figure out how it is built. Which piece should be placed at the center of the figure?

solutions.title: Find the rule
solutions.body:
- Look at two pieces that touch. On one side of the shared edge there are two circled numbers, on the other side a big number. For example, the piece with circles (5) and (11) touches the piece with 55 – and $5 \times 11 = 55$. Likewise (2)(7) sit next to 14 and (2)(13) next to 26.
- **Rule:** the two circled numbers next to an edge multiply to the number written on the other side of that edge.
- The empty spot is a triangle pointing **down**. Its neighbours:
  - Above it, the circles (3) and (17) face it, so the empty piece needs $3 \times 17 = 51$ along its top edge.
  - On its left, the piece shows 21 along the shared edge, so the empty piece needs circles whose product is 21: (3) and (7) on its left edge.
  - On its right, the piece shows 15, so it needs (3) and (5) on its right edge.
- The answer pieces are drawn pointing **up**, so turn them upside down. Turning (C) upside down puts 51 on top, (3)(7) on the left and (3)(5) on the right. ✓
- (A) turned upside down has (3)(5) on the left and (3)(7) on the right – wrong sides. (B) and (D) have 317 instead of 51, and (E) has no 51 at all.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Check the products
solutions.body:
- Every big number in the puzzle is the product of the two circled numbers across the edge: $2 \times 2 = 4$, $2 \times 13 = 26$, $2 \times 11 = 22$, $5 \times 11 = 55$, $2 \times 7 = 14$, and so on.
- The hole touches circles (3)(17), so it needs **51**, not 317 (that would be the digits written side by side). This rules out (B), (D) and (E).
- The hole's left neighbour shows **21** $= 3 \times 7$ and its right neighbour shows **15** $= 3 \times 5$.
- When we rotate a piece by half a turn to fit the down-pointing hole, its left and right sides swap. (C) has (3)(5) on the left and (3)(7) on the right, so after the half turn it has (3)(7) on the left and (3)(5) on the right – exactly what we need.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: On the larger figure on the right, Laura wants to colour in red a 2×2 square section like the one on the small figure (a 2×2 square of four cells). In how many ways can she do that?
The six smallest odd natural numbers are written on the faces of a die, in some order. Toni throws the die three times. Which of the following numbers CANNOT be the sum of the three results?

solutions.title: Odd + odd + odd
solutions.body:
- The faces are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 – all odd.
- Odd + odd = even, and even + odd = odd. So the sum of **three** odd numbers is always **odd**.
- 20 is even, so it can never be the sum.
- (The others work: $3 = 1+1+1$, $19 = 9+9+1$, $21 = 7+7+7$, $29 = 11+11+7$.)

**Answer: (C) 20**

solutions.title: Try to make each number
solutions.body:
- 3: $1 + 1 + 1$ ✓
- 19: $11 + 7 + 1$ ✓
- 21: $11 + 9 + 1$ ✓
- 29: $11 + 9 + 9$ ✓
- 20: we would need an even total, but pairs of odd numbers give even, and adding a third odd number always makes it odd again. ✗

**Answer: (C) 20**

prompt: In a family of kangaroos, the sum of the ages of all members is 36 years. After two years, the sum of their ages will be 60 years. How many kangaroos are there in this family?

solutions.title: Each kangaroo adds 2 years
solutions.body:
- In two years, every kangaroo gets 2 years older.
- The total grows from 36 to 60, which is $60 - 36 = 24$ years.
- Each kangaroo adds 2 years, so there are $24 \div 2 = 12$ kangaroos.

**Answer: (B) 12**

solutions.title: Check an answer
solutions.body:
- Try 12 kangaroos: their ages total 36 now. After 2 years each is 2 years older, adding $12 \times 2 = 24$. New total: $36 + 24 = 60$ ✓.
- With 10 kangaroos we'd get $36 + 20 = 56$, and with 15 we'd get $36 + 30 = 66$ – both wrong.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt: The following five structures were made by gluing together identical cubes. Their bases are the same and consist of eight cubes. Michael plans to paint their entire surfaces with one layer of paint. Which structure needs the most paint?

solutions.title: Look from three directions
solutions.body:
- Each base is 2 cubes wide and 4 cubes long. On the left half, every structure has a full wall that is 2 cubes high.
- For a "staircase" shape, the painted squares are exactly what you see from the top and bottom, the front and back, and the left and right: $2 \times (\text{top} + \text{front} + \text{side})$.
- Top view: 8 squares for all of them. Side view: 4 long, 2 high = 8 squares for all of them.
- Front view: (B) shows 3 squares (its right half is only 1 high), so (B) needs $2 \times (8 + 3 + 8) = 38$. (C), (D) and (E) show 4 squares, so they need $2 \times (8 + 4 + 8) = 40$.
- (A) also shows 4 squares from the front, **but** it has a hollow notch in the right half (a high cube at the front, two low cubes, then a high cube at the back). The two walls facing into the notch can't be seen from any of the six directions, but they still need paint. So (A) needs $40 + 2 = 42$.

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Count faces of structure (A)
solutions.body:
- (A) has 8 base cubes plus 6 on top (4 on the left, 2 on the right at the front and back): 14 cubes with $14 \times 6 = 84$ faces.
- Glued pairs hide 2 faces each: 10 pairs in the base, 6 cube-on-cube pairs, and 5 pairs in the top layer – 21 pairs, hiding 42 faces.
- Painted: $84 - 42 = 42$ squares.
- Doing the same for (B) (12 cubes, 17 glued pairs) gives $72 - 34 = 38$, and (C), (D), (E) each give 40. The notch in (A) is what adds the extra paint.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: On each of three pieces of paper, a three-digit number is written. The sum of the three numbers is 826. The picture shows the pieces in a position where two of the digits are covered. What is the sum of these two digits?
Riri the frog usually eats 5 spiders a day. When Riri is very hungry, she eats 10 spiders a day. Last month, she ate 60 spiders in 9 days. How many of these days was she very hungry?

solutions.title: Start with ordinary days
solutions.body:
- If all 9 days were ordinary, Riri would eat $9 \times 5 = 45$ spiders.
- She actually ate 60, which is $60 - 45 = 15$ more.
- Each very hungry day gives $10 - 5 = 5$ extra spiders, so there were $15 \div 5 = 3$ hungry days.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Check with a table
solutions.body:
- 3 hungry days: $3 \times 10 = 30$ spiders.
- 6 ordinary days: $6 \times 5 = 30$ spiders.
- Total $30 + 30 = 60$ spiders in $3 + 6 = 9$ days ✓.

**Answer: (C) 3**

In the garden of a witch there were 30 animals: dogs, cats and mice. The witch turned 6 dogs into cats. Then she turned 5 cats into mice. Now in her garden, there are the same number of dogs, cats and mice. How many cats were there at the beginning?

The cube shown in the figure has a positive integer number written on each face. The products of the two numbers on opposite faces are the same. What is the smallest possible sum of the six numbers on the cube?
Six identical black beads and three identical white beads are arranged on weighing scales as shown below. What is the total weight of these nine beads?

solutions.title: Use the right-hand scale
solutions.body:
- Right-hand scale: 3 black + 1 white on one side, 1 black + 30 g on the other.
- Take one black bead off each side: **2 black + 1 white = 30 g**.
- The nine beads are 6 black + 3 white, which is three groups of (2 black + 1 white).
- So they weigh $3 \times 30 = 90$ g.

**Answer: (E) 90 g**

solutions.title: Find each bead's weight
solutions.body:
- Left-hand scale: 2 black = 2 white + 6 g, so one black bead is 3 g heavier than one white bead.
- From the right-hand scale (after removing a black bead from each side): 2 black + 1 white = 30 g.
- Replace each black by "white + 3": $2 \times (\text{white} + 3) + \text{white} = 30$, so $3 \times \text{white} = 24$ and a white bead weighs 8 g. A black bead weighs 11 g.
- Total: $6 \times 11 + 3 \times 8 = 66 + 24 = 90$ g.

**Answer: (E) 90 g**

prompt: AliBaba and 40 thieves equally divided 42 identical bags of gold coins. Each of them got one full bag and two coins. How many coins did a bag contain?

solutions.title: The extra bag
solutions.body:
- There are $1 + 40 = 41$ people and 42 bags.
- Each person gets one full bag, using 41 bags. One bag is left over.
- The coins in that last bag are shared out: 2 coins for each of the 41 people.
- So the bag holds $41 \times 2 = 82$ coins.

**Answer: (C) 82**

solutions.title: Count all the coins
solutions.body:
- Let a bag contain $b$ coins. Total coins: $42b$.
- Each of the 41 people gets $b + 2$ coins, so the total is also $41 \times (b + 2) = 41b + 82$.
- $42b = 41b + 82$, so $b = 82$.

**Answer: (C) 82**

prompt: Robert made 5 statements (A) - (E), exactly one of which is false. Which one?
There are 11 wagons on the train, 350 passengers are traveling in them. In any three consecutive wagons there are 99 passengers. How many passengers are in the sixth wagon?

solutions.title: Group the wagons in threes
solutions.body:
- Wagons 1–3, 4–6 and 7–9 each hold 99 passengers: $3 \times 99 = 297$.
- So wagons 10 and 11 hold $350 - 297 = 53$.
- Wagons 9, 10, 11 also hold 99, so wagon 9 has $99 - 53 = 46$.
- Wagons 4–6 and wagons 5–7 both have 99, so wagon 4 = wagon 7. In the same way wagon 6 = wagon 9. So wagon 6 has **46** passengers.

**Answer: (D) 46**

solutions.title: Spot the repeating pattern
solutions.body:
- Wagons 1–3 and 2–4 both total 99, so wagon 1 = wagon 4. Likewise each wagon equals the one 3 places later.
- So the numbers repeat: $a, b, c, a, b, c, a, b, c, a, b$ with $a + b + c = 99$.
- Total: $4a + 4b + 3c = 4 \times (a + b + c) - c = 396 - c = 350$, so $c = 46$.
- Wagon 6 is a "$c$" wagon, so it has 46 passengers.

**Answer: (D) 46**

prompt: With blocks of dimension 1 cm × 1 cm × 2 cm, you can build towers as shown in the picture. How high is a tower that is built in the same way with 28 blocks?

solutions.title: Count blocks and layers
solutions.body:
- Standing blocks are 2 cm high, lying blocks are 1 cm high. Layers alternate: standing, lying, standing, ...
- Blocks in the towers shown: $3 = 2+1$, $6 = 3+2+1$, $10 = 4+3+2+1$, $15 = 5+4+3+2+1$.
- Continue: $21 = 6+5+\dots+1$, then $28 = 7+6+5+4+3+2+1$. So the 28-block tower has 7 layers.
- Layers from the bottom: standing (2), lying (1), standing (2), lying (1), standing (2), lying (1), standing (2).
- Height: $4 \times 2 + 3 \times 1 = 11$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 11 cm**

solutions.title: Height pattern
solutions.body:
- Heights of the towers shown: 3 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, 8 cm. Each new tower adds one layer, alternately 2 cm (standing) or 1 cm (lying): +2, +1, +2, ...
- Tower 5 (21 blocks): $8 + 1 = 9$ cm. Tower 6 (28 blocks): $9 + 2 = 11$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 11 cm**

Cathie wrote some numbers at the vertices of the cube. Then she calculated the sums of numbers on the left, on the right and on the top faces. She got values 14, 22 and 18 respectively. What is the sum of the numbers on the lower face?

solutions.title: Opposite faces cover all corners
solutions.body:
- A cube has 8 corners. The left face and the right face are opposite, and together they contain **all 8 corners** exactly once.
- So the sum of all 8 numbers is $14 + 22 = 36$.
- The top face and the bottom face are also opposite and also cover all 8 corners once. So top + bottom = 36.
- Bottom $= 36 - 18 = 18$.

**Answer: (B) 18**

solutions.title: Try an example
solutions.body:
- Put the numbers 1, 2, 3, 8 on the left face (sum 14) and 4, 5, 6, 7 on the right face (sum 22).
- The top face uses two corners from the left face and two from the right face; the bottom face uses the other four.
- Whatever the top four add to (here 18), the bottom four must add to the rest of the total $14 + 22 = 36$, i.e. $36 - 18 = 18$.

**Answer: (B) 18**

On most digital clocks, the time is displayed by four digits – the first two showing the hours, and the last two showing the minutes. Every digit is displayed by at most 7 segments, some of which are off (invisible) and some are on (visible), as follows (see the figure). Unfortunately, for all four of the digits on Mark's digital clock, the same two segments are broken and cannot be switched on if needed. At this moment Mark's clock shows the time in the figure. What will the clock show in 3 hours and 45 minutes?

solutions.title: Find the broken segments
solutions.body:
- The last digit shows only the top bar and the lower-right bar. No digit looks like that, so it must be a **7** with its **upper-right** segment broken.
- The first digit shows top, middle and bottom bars only. With the upper-right broken, this must be a **2** whose **lower-left** segment is also broken (a 3 would also light the lower-right bar, and that bar works – the second digit shows it).
- So the broken segments are upper-right and lower-left. Then the second digit (top, middle, bottom, lower-right) is a **3**, and the third digit (upper-left, middle, lower-right) is a **4**.
- The time now is **23:47**. In 3 hours 45 minutes it will be $23{:}47 + 3{:}45 = 27{:}32$, i.e. **03:32**.
- Draw 0, 3, 3, 2 without the upper-right and lower-left segments: that's picture (A).

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Check the answer pictures
solutions.body:
- Once we know the clock shows 23:47 (with the upper-right and lower-left segments broken), the new time is 03:32.
- Without the upper-right and lower-left segments: a 0 shows top, upper-left, lower-right and bottom; a 3 shows top, middle, lower-right and bottom; a 2 shows only top, middle and bottom.
- Picture (A) shows exactly these four digits. In (B) the second digit also lights the upper-left bar, which a 3 never uses, and (C), (D), (E) have digits that don't fit 0, 3, 3, 2 at all.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Zev has two machines: one exchanges 1 white token into 4 red tokens, while the other exchanges 1 red token into 3 white ones. Zev starts with 4 white tokens. After exactly 11 exchanges, he has 31 tokens. How many of those are red?

solutions.title: Count how the total grows
solutions.body:
- White → 4 red: one token becomes 4, so the total goes **up by 3**.
- Red → 3 white: one token becomes 3, so the total goes **up by 2**.
- The total grew from 4 to 31, i.e. by 27, in 11 exchanges. If all 11 were "+2" exchanges, it would grow by 22. The extra $27 - 22 = 5$ means 5 exchanges were "+3" (white → red) and 6 were "+2" (red → white).
- Red tokens: made $5 \times 4 = 20$, used up 6. So $20 - 6 = 14$ red tokens.
- Check: white tokens $4 - 5 + 6 \times 3 = 17$, and $14 + 17 = 31$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) 14**

solutions.title: Try the numbers
solutions.body:
- Let $w$ = number of white→red exchanges and $r$ = number of red→white exchanges, with $w + r = 11$.
- Total tokens: $4 + 3w + 2r = 31$, so $3w + 2r = 27$.
- Try $w = 5$, $r = 6$: $15 + 12 = 27$ ✓.
- Red tokens: $4w - r = 20 - 6 = 14$.

**Answer: (C) 14**
